Three people in the Andheri flat were paying for three separate data packs on their phones, and each bought their own rice, oil and dal in small packets from the corner shop. One Sunday Zubin wrote it all on the fridge whiteboard: ₹1,800 a month on data between them, and the corner shop's grocery receipts beside it.
Step one: he proposed a single home broadband connection, ₹750 a month split three ways. Arohi agreed at once. Fardeen wanted a month to test the speed first.
Step two: a shared staples list, bought once a month from the wholesale market at Vashi.
The first trip fell on the wettest Saturday of July. The train was packed, and Zubin and Arohi came back soaked, carrying a 25-kilo rice sack between them. But the receipt, pinned beside the list, showed the same staples for about a third less than the corner shop charged.
Fardeen tested the broadband for a month and stayed in.

Gurleen frowned. 'I eat at the office most days. Why should I pay a third for rice?'
'Then you pay for what you use. Internet a third each, staples split between Nitin and me, and you just chip in for tea and sugar.'
Gurleen agreed to that. The first Begum Bazaar trip took a whole Sunday morning. By month end, Vikas's notebook showed ₹1,400 less spent than in October, on exactly the same food.

Mentor's note, 28 February. Karthik, graduate-trainee mentor.
Dolma came to our fortnightly chat a little sheepish. In January she ran a very strict budget: no eating out, no shopping, not even tea at the stall downstairs. She was proud of it for three weeks. Then, on the last Saturday, she bought a ₹7,000 jacket and two pairs of shoes online in one evening, and the month ended worse than December.
'I don't know what happened,' she said. 'I was being so good.'
We talked it through. She decided on her own that February would include a ₹1,500 'fun line' for tea, one movie and small things, planned and guilt-free. Today she showed me: ₹1,340 used, no late-night shopping, and savings slightly up on January.
She laughed that the tea tasted better now that it was allowed. I'll ask about March at our next meeting.

qa.a: A ₹1,500 'fun line'.

qa.q: How did Dolma feel coming to the chat after January?
qa.a: She was sheepish and confused, since she felt she had been 'so good' and still ended the month worse.

qa.a: Whether the fun line still feels like enough, adjusting it a little if cravings build again rather than going back to zero.

Sunday, 3 November. Jyoti's diary.
Confession first. October was my 'zero fun' month. No cafés, no shopping, cooked every meal. I felt like a monk and was very proud of it.
Then on the 30th, after a horrible week at work, I bought wireless earbuds, a perfume and a hoodie, all at midnight. ₹6,200. More than I'd saved all month by being a monk.
Lokesh bhaiya laughed on the phone and said, 'You starved yourself and then ate the whole buffet.' Annoying, but true.
So November's plan has a new line: 'fun, ₹1,200'. Planned. Chai with Neelam on Fridays, one movie, maybe earrings. If it runs out, it runs out.
Weird to write 'fun' in a budget. It feels like permission. Maybe that's what I was missing.

The placement cell's waiting room smelled of printer toner. Karthik had a campus offer letter in one hand and his loan papers in the other, and while they waited for the counsellor he worked it out aloud for Chaitanya.
'Six lakh, total. The bank says seven years to repay, starting after the grace period. So the end date is fixed. Work backward. Eighty-four months. Without interest that's about seven thousand a month. With interest, the bank sheet says close to ten thousand.'
'And the offer?'
'Thirty-five thousand in hand.' He stopped. 'So nearly a third of my salary, every month, for seven years.'
Chaitanya whistled.
'No, it's useful. Now I know the rent I can afford is whatever fits after that ten thousand. Not before.'
When his name was called, Karthik had one question circled to ask: whether the bank allowed paying extra later without charges.

The bank says my ₹6 lakh loan must be closed in seven years from next June. With interest, that's about ₹10,000 a month. That number is fixed, so everything else has to fit around it.

Anirban, before you sign anything, sit down. Your Pema aunty took an education loan too, back when I went to Pune for nursing.
Everyone told me what to do. Pay it fast, pay it slow, don't pay anything till you get a job. I was confused, so I did one thing first. I took the sanction letter to the bank and sat at the loan officer's desk with a notebook.
I wrote down four things. The interest rate: ten and a half percent. When the grace period ended: six months after the course. The EMI after that. And whether I'd be charged for paying early. That last one I didn't understand, so I asked the officer to explain it twice, slowly.
Only after that page was full did I decide anything. Now it's your turn, Anirban. Where is your sanction letter?

Avni reached the branch at 1:40, twenty minutes before the loan desk shut for lunch, with her sanction letter in a plastic folder and six people ahead of her in the queue.
She used the wait. On the back of the folder she wrote four headings: rate, when the moratorium ends, EMI, charges for paying early. Then she hunted for each one in the letter. Rate: 9.8 percent, floating. Moratorium: ends twelve months after the course. EMI: ₹7,900 after that. Prepayment: one clause she couldn't make sense of.
At 1:58 she reached the desk. The officer, Nandini, glanced at the clock. Avni held up the folder. 'Just one thing. What does this line about part-payment mean?'
Nandini read it and explained: no charge for paying extra on a floating rate. Avni wrote 'NONE' in capitals.
The shutter came down behind her. Only now, with all four boxes filled, would she start thinking about a plan.

'Loan first, obviously,' said Simran from the sofa. 'It's bigger.'
'Bigger, yes.' Sharmila tapped the passbook. 'Four lakh at about nine percent a year.' She tapped the statement. 'Twenty-two thousand at about three and a half percent a month. That's over forty a year.'
She worked it roughly aloud. 'Every thousand on the card costs me around thirty-five rupees a month. Every thousand on the loan costs about seven or eight. So the card is eating me alive and the loan is just nibbling.'
She paid the whole ₹8,000 onto the card that evening. 'Three months like this and it's gone. Then the extra goes to the loan.'
Simran looked up. 'When did you get so good at this?'

Vijay has been jumpy at his desk this week, turning his phone face down whenever it buzzed. The bank called today. Not a message, an actual person. My first EMI was due on the 7th. I didn't pay it because I didn't know it was due, because I haven't opened a single bank message since March. I saw 'education loan' in the preview and swiped them away. Every one.

'The company mailed again,' Santosh said at dinner. 'Joining is pushed to March now.'
Pankaj, his father, put the roti down. 'And the loan EMI starts in January.'
'I know. I was thinking I'd just borrow from Mama for two months and not tell the bank.'
'And if March becomes May?'
Santosh was quiet. 'Then I'd be stuck.'
'So who should know first?'
'The bank.' He rubbed his face. 'Tomorrow I'll go to the branch. Take the offer letter and the delay mail.'
'What will you ask?'
'Whether the start can move, or the tenure get longer so the EMI is smaller for a while. Whatever options they have.'
The next evening he was back. 'The manager said coming before a missed payment makes a real difference. They're reviewing a three-month extension of the moratorium. I have to send the documents by Friday.'
Pankaj nodded. 'Good. Send them Thursday.'

I'm Shalini. Last December my offer letter said I'd start on 2 January. Then HR sent a one-line mail: onboarding postponed, 'likely April'. My EMI of ₹8,200 was due from 15 January.
My first thought was to stay silent and scrape it together somehow. My cousin had done that. Then my friend Samir told me his elder brother had tried the same and ended up with late fees stacked three months deep.

The officer read both, asked about my savings, and explained two options: a short extra moratorium, or a longer tenure with a smaller EMI. I chose the moratorium till April.
The officer said most people come in after missing three payments. I came in before missing one.

Jatin's first salary as a lab assistant would be ₹19,000. ₹4,300 sounded like something he could forget about. He signed for fifteen years without reading the second page.

I'm Reena, and in March I got my first bonus: ₹60,000. The question was whether to put it into my education loan early or keep it.
So I made a list in two columns on the office whiteboard after hours.
For prepaying: less interest over the years, loan finished sooner, one less thing on my mind.
For keeping it: the interest on this loan gets a tax deduction, so it costs a bit less than the rate says; and I have almost no emergency savings.
My senior, Tarun, looked at it and said he'd kept his loan running for the deduction, but his situation was different: he already had savings. Then I booked a session with a fee-only adviser, someone paid by the hour who doesn't sell anything. The adviser asked for my actual numbers and went through them with me.
The list didn't decide for me. But I understood what I was choosing.

Shalini brought a pros-and-cons list to our monthly chat. She has an education loan and ₹50,000 saved, and wanted to know whether to prepay part of the loan.
